title: Delta Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Delta wells have a 37-foot median depth, but buyers should check yield, water levels, permits and nearby environmental sites.
h1: What Delta, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Delta means looking beyond the presence of a well. Colorado DWR records show 498 permitted wells within 5 miles of Delta, with 309 recorded as constructed. Only 48 report a pump yield and 18 report a static water level, so the records are useful for local patterns but cannot answer every question about a particular property.

Most recorded wells are shallow, and reported yields are generally strong. Still, the aquifer is commonly listed as unnamed or fractured bedrock, and individual lots can behave differently. Use neighboring well records, a current pump test, water-quality testing and a proper site review before you commit to a property or construction plan.

sections.heading: Delta well depth: shallow is common, but not guaranteed
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Delta is 37 feet. The middle half runs from 21 to 52 feet, and 94% of the recorded wells are under 100 feet. That is a favorable starting point when asking for a drilling bid in the Delta area, including toward Orchard City and Olathe.

There are exceptions. The deepest recorded well is 470 feet, while 4% fall between 100 and 300 feet and 2% between 300 and 600 feet. A driller should price the actual ground at your lot, not simply use the local median. Permits most often name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 478 wells in that category. Sedimentary and alluvial conditions can still change quickly from one parcel to the next.

sections.heading: Reported Delta well yields are usually useful for homes
sections.html:
Among the 48 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 14.8 to 21.2 gallons per minute, and 75% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 2% are under 1 gallon per minute, with another 2% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

Those figures suggest that a typical reported well can support ordinary household use, but yield is not the same as storage or guaranteed daily supply. Ask for the well construction report, pump test and production history. An exempt household-use well is generally subject to Colorado’s 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Irrigation, livestock and other uses may require different permit terms or an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: Delta water levels are shallow, but the trend is unclear
sections.html:
The 18 records reporting a static water level show a median depth to water of 7 feet, with the middle half from 6 to 9 feet. That shallow water level can reduce drilling depth, but it also deserves attention during excavation, trenching and basement planning. Water levels can vary with season, pumping and local conditions.

Permit activity spans the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2024. That permit history does not establish a falling or rising water table because the available static-water-level records are limited and are not presented as a consistent time series. Have the current owner document water level and pump performance rather than relying only on the local median.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Delta, and what the permit history shows
sections.html:
Recorded drilling activity has continued across several decades. The largest decade totals are 89 permits in the 1990s, 87 in the 2000s, 67 in the 1970s, 48 in the 1980s, 46 in the 2010s and 21 in the 2020s. These figures describe permits in the five-mile search area, not necessarily completed or currently operating wells.

The most active named driller in the records is K. W. Anderson Drilling, listed as Anderson, Kermit W, with 54 records. Authorized, listed as Pe, Pg, has 52, and Bill Kissner Drilling Inc, listed as Kissner, Bill F., has 26. Treat those names as historical permit information, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, availability, scope and references before hiring anyone.

sections.heading: A Delta well may cost less to drill than to finish
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground reported around Delta, the drilling rate model is $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 37 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $1,800 to $2,800. That is only the hole, not a working water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $7,800 to $14,800 at the median depth. The final bid can change with access, casing and grout requirements, pump size, trench length, power service and site conditions. Ask the driller to separate drilling, casing, development, pump equipment, electrical and testing so an apparently low bid does not leave out necessary work.

sections.heading: Delta risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. Records show 18 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 22 historic mine features and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. That does not prove a particular well is affected, but it is enough reason to test the water and investigate the property’s direction from known sites. A certified laboratory can test for common household concerns and site-specific contaminants.

Also verify the well permit, construction report, casing and grout details, pump equipment, pressure tank and recent service history. A shallow water level may complicate septic and foundation work if excavation reaches groundwater. Check septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, drainage, access for a drilling rig and the proposed building location before finalizing plans.

sections.heading: What to do before buying a Delta lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare nearby permitted wells rather than relying on the town-wide median. Records from Orchard City, Olathe, Cedaredge, Lazear, Hotchkiss and Montrose can provide broader regional context, but the closest wells are usually more useful for estimating depth, aquifer behavior and construction conditions.

For an existing home, make the purchase contingent on reviewing the permit, testing the water and checking pump output under use. For vacant land, have a driller review access, likely well location, septic layout and power route before you set a house plan. Confirm whether the intended domestic, stock or irrigation use is allowed. If the basin is over-appropriated, ask Colorado DWR or a water attorney whether an augmentation plan is required.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Delta, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Delta is 37 feet. The middle half ranges from 21 to 52 feet, and 94% are under 100 feet. The deepest recorded well is 470 feet, so a shallow local average does not guarantee the same result on every parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Delta, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 37-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,800 to $2,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $7,800 to $14,800. Access and site conditions can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Delta wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 48 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 14.8 to 21.2 gallons per minute, and 75% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 2% report under 1 gallon per minute, but a property-specific pump test is still important.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Delta, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles are 18 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 22 historic mine features and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well through a certified laboratory, especially before buying or occupying a property.

faq.q: Are Delta, Colorado wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available records show a median static water level of 7 feet, with the middle half from 6 to 9 feet, but only 18 wells report that measurement. The data does not provide a reliable time trend showing a falling water table. Get a current water-level and pump-performance check for the specific property.
